newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Britain seeks to exempt BSE-free herds from EU ban. [CORRECTED 01:50 GMT 10/10/96]
newsitem.headline: Britain seeks to exempt BSE-free herds from EU ban. [CORRECTED 01:50 GMT 10/10/96]

text.p: Britain has submitted a proposal to the European Commission for exempting grass-fed herds that are free of mad cow disease from a worldwide export ban, a senior British agricultural official said on Tuesday.

The EU's executive imposed the ban in March to protect public health after the British government admitted that the disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), could be transmitted to humans who ate infected beef.

"We are trying to act for the whole of the UK," Richard Packer, Permanent Secretary in the British Ministry of Agriculture, told reporters after giving evidence to the European Parliament's committee of inquiry into BSE.

"It ought to be possible to make progress on Northern Ireland and for example the Scottish islands," added Packer who represented the British government after Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg declined to attend.
Northern Irish farmers in particular have campaigned hard for exemption from the crippling ban, pointing to a computerised system for identifying and tracing animals from birth.

Packer, who said that British and Commission officials were expected to discuss the proposal next week, added that London had not ruled out the possibility of speeding up the cull in some regions so as to comply with EU conditions.
Britain last month shelved the start-up of a programme imposed by the EU to slaughter up to 147,000 extra cattle at risk to the fatal brain wasting disease.
The cull was in addition to the slaughter of animals over the age of 30 months of age and destruction of the carcasses to prevent them entering the food chain.

Britain has so far killed almost 600,000 (Corrects from over 190,000) such animals of which 80 percent were found to be infected with BSE. But there is a backlog of around 400,000 animals waiting to be slaughtered.
Packer stressed that Britain had not broken a commitment made at an EU summit in Florence to carry out the selective cull as part of a deal for a gradual lifting of the ban.
"We have not said we will not proceed," he said, noting that the Florence agreement allowed for the cull to be adjusted to take account of scientific developments.
An Oxford University study published in August said that BSE will be virtually eradicated by 2001, regardless of any cull.
Asked by the inquiry committee if the British government was to blame for BSE, Packer said, "It was an act of God."
But noting that BSE was a new and unprecedented disease, he said that some matters might now have been handled differently.

Mad cow disease was rapidly declining and will disappear in Britain as a result of national measures, he said, adding that the major tasks were now to continue protecting public health and to restore confidence in beef.
